power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Using a magnet and a mind, we revealed the brain's somatotopic organization without touching the body.
Fingertip representations were first mapped using vibrotactile stimulation at 7T, then again by directing attention across the fingers under constant vibration.
Finally, attention was directed to the fingertips and facial regions using only auditory cues, without any external tactile stimulation.
Prior training in a sensoryrestricted float tank subjectively sharpened attentional precision and bodily awareness.
Remarkably, somatotopic maps emerged in the absence of external tactile stimulation -showing that structured attention alone can reveal the brain's somatotopic organization.
The 7T MRI was a dark tunnel of hums and beeps, and unlike any 3T scanner I had entered, the magnetic intensity was palpable.
As the bed advanced, it felt less like translation through space than a subtle rotation, as though I were being gently corkscrewed in.
This time, unlike prior somatosensory experiments, there was to be no stimulation.
Instead the experiment was reduced to its simplest elements: attention, timing, and the body itself.

Under these conditions, activity in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) would be shaped not by physical stimulation, but by sustained, deliberate shifts of attention across the body -a concept supported by early physiological studies showing attention dependent tuning of somatosensory responses in humans (Roland, 1981).
text.formatted: Under these conditions, activity in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) would be shaped not by physical stimulation, but by sustained, deliberate shifts of attention across the body -a concept supported by early physiological studies showing attention dependent tuning of somatosensory responses in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Roland, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: The groundwork for this had already been laid.

In an earlier experiment we had mapped the terrain of my fingertips using phase-encoded vibrotactile stimulation (Puckett et al., 2017), revealing fine-scale somatotopic gradients in S1 (Figure 1) similar to other high-resolution mapping work (e.g., Sanchez-Panchuelo et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In an earlier experiment we had mapped the terrain of my fingertips using phase-encoded vibrotactile stimulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Puckett et al., 2017)</ref>, revealing fine-scale somatotopic gradients in S1 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) similar to other high-resolution mapping work (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Sanchez-Panchuelo et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Functional MRI (fMRI) imaged blood oxygenation, a proxy for neural activity, tracing activation from fingertip to fingertip.
For a contemporary synthesis of methods in human somatosensory fMRI, see Puckett & Sanchez-Panchuelo (2023).
text.formatted: For a contemporary synthesis of methods in human somatosensory fMRI, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Puckett & Sanchez-Panchuelo (2023)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this foundation of stimulus-driven fingertip maps, we next tested whether internally directed attention could reproduce the same somatotopic patterns.
All fingers were held under constant vibrotactile stimulation while attention was swept across them, following the same phase-encoded timing as the previous stimulation.

Remarkably, this attentional sweep reproduced the topography observed during physical stimulation (Figure 2) -demonstrating that attention, when structured in time, can modulate somatosensory cortical responses under uniform sensory input (Puckett et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Remarkably, this attentional sweep reproduced the topography observed during physical stimulation (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>) -demonstrating that attention, when structured in time, can modulate somatosensory cortical responses under uniform sensory input <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Puckett et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The next step removed external stimulation altogether.
In the scanner, without any tactile input to the fingertips, I followed auditory timing cues to shift attention from fingertip to fingertip.
The resulting map aligned with those obtained during both physical stimulation and attention under constant vibration -showing the same orderly representation of fingertips (Figure 3).
text.formatted: The resulting map aligned with those obtained during both physical stimulation and attention under constant vibration -showing the same orderly representation of fingertips (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Encouraged by this consistency, we extended the approach to the face, directing attention sequentially to the brow, nostril, upper lip, and tongue.
Each location elicited activation in the somatotopic territory of S1 (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Each location elicited activation in the somatotopic territory of S1 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Viewed at a broader scale, these fingertip and face maps occupied their canonical positions along the postcentral gyrus, arranged where classical homuncular organization would predict (cf. inflated cortical surfaces in Figures 1 2 3vs.
text.formatted: Viewed at a broader scale, these fingertip and face maps occupied their canonical positions along the postcentral gyrus, arranged where classical homuncular organization would predict (cf. inflated cortical surfaces in Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>vs.

text.text: Figure 4; Penfield & Rasmussen, 1950).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Penfield & Rasmussen, 1950)</ref>.

text.text: Seen together, the results illustrate a simple but striking point: somatotopy can be revealed not only using stimulation, but also through temporally structured attention to the body.
The subjective experience provided additional insight.
Attending to the nostril produced sensations that were expected: the passage of air with each inhalation and exhalation.
Less expected, at least prior to training, was that sustained attention to the fingertips brought with it a clear awareness of the ebb and flow of each breath throughout the hands.
With each respiratory cycle, subtle pressure changes became apparent across the body, linking distant regions through shared internal rhythms.
Blood pulsed, gravity persisted, and these bodily signals provided a continuous backdrop against which attention could be placed and held.
This precision was not accidental.

Over the two months prior to scanning, I trained roughly twice per week in a sensory-restricted float tank, deliberately practicing the ability to shift and hold attention on specific body regions without tactile input.

I used the same auditory sequence later employed in the scanner: one high-pitched tone followed by three low-pitched tones, with the high tone serving as a checkpoint to confirm attention was correctly placed.
If attention drifted or fatigue set in, the high tone prompted reorientation.

Staying attentive in near-total sensory deprivation was initially difficult, but lapses became less frequent, and by the time of scanning, attention could be confidently sustained until the next tone.
In the end, the experiments demonstrated that orderly somatotopic maps need not depend on external stimulation, but can be revealed through sustained attentional control.
With only beeps and intention, somatotopic organization emerged -without cables, stimulators, or the specialised equipment normally required to deliver tactile input in a 7T environment.
Attention proved to be the simplest tool of all: inexpensive, portable, and remarkably effective.
The brain, it seems, does not merely register the body when the world presses upon it; given the right conditions, it can reveal its own maps from within.

Figure 1.
Fingertip map -stimulation.
Left: schematic showing phase-encoded vibrotactile stimulation delivered across four fingertips (colors indicate timing).
Five cycles were delivered while remaining passive.
Right, bottom: inflated cortical surface showing somatosensory activation along the post-central gyrus (unthresholded, warm colors indicate correlation ³ 0.5).
Right, top: zoomed-in delay map (thresholded at q = 0.05) revealing orderly fingertip representations.
Data previously published in Puckett et al.
Figure 2.
Fingertip map -attention with external stimulation.
Left: schematic illustrating phase-encoded shifts of attention across the four fingertips while all fingers received continuous vibrotactile stimulation.
Attention followed the same temporal structure as the stimulation cycles used in Figure 1.
Right, bottom: inflated cortical surface showing position of activation.
Right, top: zoomed-in delay map showing fingertip representations derived from attention, closely matching that obtained during direct stimulation.
Data published in Puckett et al.
Figure 3.
Fingertip map -attention without external stimulation.
Left: schematic depicting phase-encoded shifts of attention across four fingertips in the absence of any tactile stimulation.
Attention was guided along the same temporal structure as in Figures 1-2.
Right, bottom: inflated cortical surface showing position of activation.
Right, top: delay map showing orderly fingertip representation elicited by attention alone.
Figure 4.
Face map -attention without external stimulation.
Left: schematic showing phase-encoded shifts of attention across face regions (brow, nostril, upper lip, tongue) without tactile stimulation.
The attentional sweep followed the same temporal structure used in Figures 1-3.
Right, bottom: inflated cortical surface showing somatosensory activation in inferior face regions.
Right, top: zoomed-in delay map revealing clear somatotopic organization.
